          "text": "# OCL 269: A Cluster on Cassiopeia\u2019s Edge\n\n**Dek:** Near the northern sky\u2019s familiar W, this broad open cluster rewards patient sweeping more than high magnification.\n\nSome deep-sky objects announce themselves with a sharp outline. OCL 269, listed in SIMBAD as the open cluster NGC 7789, is subtler: a spread of starlight in Cassiopeia that asks you to slow down and let the field resolve. Its position\u2014right ascension 23h 57m 20.2s, declination +56\u00b0 43\u2032 34\u2033\u2014puts it in a rich northern region of the Milky Way. [SIMBAD\u2019s NGC 7789 entry](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%207789) classifies it as an open cluster.\n\nAn open cluster is a gathering of stars associated by their shared origin, rather than a distant galaxy or a compact ball of ancient stars. SIMBAD gives this one an apparent diameter of about 25.3 arcminutes\u2014close to the full Moon\u2019s width on the sky. That breadth is a clue to how to observe it: this is not a target to squeeze into the highest-power eyepiece. Use a wide field, and give your eyes time to notice the small points emerging from the background.\n\nThe catalogue also lists a parallax of 0.453 milliarcseconds. Taking the inverse gives a rough distance of about 2,200 parsecs, or 7,200 light-years. That is an estimate from the listed parallax, not a claim that every cluster star sits at precisely the same distance. SIMBAD records a radial velocity of about \u201355 kilometres per second, measured relative to the Sun. The minus sign means the measured motion along our line of sight is toward us; it does not describe the cluster\u2019s full motion across the sky.\n\nFor observing, start with Cassiopeia\u2019s unmistakable W shape and use a current star chart or planetarium app to guide you from its bright stars to the cluster\u2019s coordinates. Because the cluster lies far north, it is well placed for many northern observers, especially on clear autumn evenings. From a dark site, try binoculars first: 7\u00d750 or 10\u00d750 binoculars offer a generous field and can reveal the cluster as a concentrated, grainy patch. A small telescope at low power should make the impression more granular; increase magnification only if the view remains comfortably framed.\n\nSIMBAD lists a V magnitude of 6.7, but flags that photometric value with low quality. In any case, a cluster\u2019s light is spread across its apparent area, so a single brightness number cannot promise a naked-eye sighting. Light pollution, transparency and the observer\u2019s adaptation to darkness matter. Shield nearby lights, avoid looking at a bright phone screen, and let your vision settle for several minutes. If the first view looks like a haze, keep observing: faint stars often appear one by one as your gaze moves gently around the field.\n\nOCL 269\u2019s appeal is not a dramatic silhouette. It is the gradual transformation of a pale patch into a crowd of separate suns\u2014a small, satisfying lesson in what patient observing can uncover."
